analysis.one_liner: Requires congressional districts to be drawn by independent citizen commissions, once per decade.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have taken congressional map-drawing away from state legislators, was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require every state to draw its congressional district lines through an independent redistricting commission made up of citizens rather than through bills passed by the state legislature. It would bar states from redrawing congressional maps more than once after each ten-year census, except when a court orders a redo to comply with the Constitution or the Voting Rights Act. It sets rules for how commissions must work — open meetings, public websites where anyone can draw and submit maps, and a ban on using voters' party affiliation or the home addresses of sitting members of Congress when drawing lines — and sends federal money to states to run the commissions. If a state legislature rejects the commission's plan, the state's highest court picks among the commission's plans, and if it does not, a federal court draws the map.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters gain district lines that are not engineered by the party in power to be safe for its incumbents. Candidates would have to compete for votes rather than rely on maps drawn by state legislative majorities, and voters would be less locked into predictable outcomes in heavily gerrymandered states. The bill's criteria also require districts to keep counties, municipalities, and neighborhoods together where practicable, and it funds the process so small states can run commissions.

how_it_helps.text: It requires every state to use an independent redistricting commission, with members barred from having held office or worked for a party or candidate in the prior four years and barred from running for Congress until the next census, replacing map-drawing by the politicians whose own seats are at stake.

It prohibits states from redrawing congressional maps more than once after each apportionment unless a court orders it, which would stop the practice of legislatures re-gerrymandering maps mid-decade when one election gives them more power.

It bans the commission from considering voters' party affiliation, voting history, or the residence of incumbents when drawing districts, and requires open meetings, a public website with mapping software anyone can use, and public hearings around the state.
It provides $150,000 per congressional seat in federal payments to states to operate the commissions, so the process is funded without depending on the political branches of state government.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislative party leaders lose their ability to draw their own districts and lock in favorable maps. States bear the administrative work of standing up commissions under federal deadlines, and the federal cost of commission payments is authorized at 'such sums as may be necessary.' Voters in states whose legislatures would reject commission plans could end up with maps chosen by courts rather than any elected body.

drawbacks.text: The commission members are appointed by the majority and minority leaders of the state legislature's two chambers, so the same party politicians who draw maps today would choose the people who draw maps instead — a weaker form of independence than citizen-commission systems where members pick their own successors.

It overrides the procedures of all fifty states with a single federal formula, including a rule that state legislatures may only approve or reject a commission plan without amending it, which many would argue intrudes on state authority over their own elections; if a state misses the deadline to form a commission, a federal court draws its map.

A single-redistricting limit could prevent a state from promptly fixing a legally flawed or outdated map for any reason other than a court order, even if a new legislature and governor want to change it.
The effective date is after the 2030 census, so even if enacted it would not have affected any map used this decade.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — taking district-drawing away from the officeholders whose seats depend on the lines — is real and addresses a practice that has made most House seats non-competitive. The design is imperfect: members are still chosen by legislative leaders, the federal override of state processes would face both political resistance and legal challenge, and court-drawn maps are a blunt fallback. But on balance the bill targets a structural advantage held by incumbent politicians of both parties, and its costs fall mainly on them.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on April 17, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor; the bill ended the Congress with zero cosponsors.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the House floor, dying at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress and the state legislative majorities of both parties who draw congressional maps kept their control of the process, because the bill that would have taken it away never moved.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee; it gained no cosponsors in either chamber.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Jim Jordan, R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 17, 2023 and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining 20 months of the Congress.

against.name: House leadership of both parties
against.what_they_did: Neither party's leadership moved to bring redistricting-commission rules to the floor, and no member from either party cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by one Democrat with zero cosponsors from either party and was never voted on, so the record shows no party split — only a single sponsor and no floor test.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislative majorities who draw maps
industries.note: The bill strips politicians of the power to draw the congressional districts they run in, bans using incumbent residences or voter partisanship, and locks maps for the decade after each census. Their interest in keeping map-drawing power runs against voters who want competitive districts.

industries.industry: Political parties and campaign infrastructure built around safe districts
industries.note: Commission members must not have worked for a party or candidate in the prior four years, and districts could not be designed around party voting patterns, reducing the value of safe-seat incumbency and the primary-election control it gives party insiders.
